articles.title: Shohei Ohtani out of Dodgers lineup for third straight game as possible IL stint looms
articles.summary: It's unclear when Shohei Ohtani will be appearing for the Dodgers again.
articles.body:
Shohei Ohtani's absence from the Los Angeles Dodgers' lineup has reached a third straight game, with the possibility of an injured list stint seemingly becoming more real with each day.

Ohtani was once again out of the lineup for the Dodgers' game against the Washington Nationals on Saturday. Dalton Rushing was originally the replacement at designated hitter, but he was later scratched and replaced by Alex Call.

Dodgers manager Dave Roberts told reporters later Saturday that Ohtani will hit in the cage, per The Athletic's Fabian Ardaya , with his body's response deciding the next course of action, such as the IL.

Ohtani's last appearance in a game was on Wednesday, an ugly four-strikeout performance that sparked new concerns that the knee issue that has kept him off the mound since early July is starting to affect his hitting. He has slashed only .264/.344/.526 in the two months he's worked only as a designated hitter, well off his norms since joining the Dodgers, and remains only two for his last 23, with 11 strikeouts.

Roberts has gotten progressively less optimistic about Ohtani's outlook over the past few days, conceding that an IL stint was a "possibility" on Wednesday then admitting he was "hopeful" but not "confident" Ohtani would avoid such a fate .

The possibility of Ohtani returning as a pitcher appears more remote, with Roberts saying earlier this week that shutting him down for the season on the mound is "an option."

If Ohtani hits the injured list, it will be the first time he's done so since joining the Dodgers before the 2024 season. Even while recovering from internal brace surgery on the torn UCL in his pitching arm, he was still playing nearly every day as a designated hitter.

MLB rules state that injured list placements can only be backdated a maximum of three days. The Dodgers would obviously like to have Ohtani in their lineup as soon as possible, but the question will soon be whether they want to bet an entire roster spot on him becoming healthy enough within a week.

articles.title: Yankees' Trent Grisham goes on IL with right hamstring strain as Aaron Judge nears return
articles.summary: The Yankees have players to fill in for Grisham in the outfield, and AL MVP Aaron Judge could soon be among them.
articles.body:
Outfielder Trent Grisham has been placed on the 10-day injured list with a right hamstring strain, the New York Yankees announced on Saturday .

Grisham, 29, left Friday's 3-2 loss to the San Diego Padres in the second inning. After drawing a walk against Padres pitcher Walker Buehler, Grisham attempted to steal second base and was thrown out.

In the bottom of the second, Grisham played center field in the bottom of the inning. But he was clearly laboring while trying to run in on a bloop single by Xander Bogaerts and Spencer Jones shifted over to center field from right field in the third.

Grisham has 18 home runs, 19 doubles and 59 RBI this season, but is slashing .211/.308/.395 in 484 plate appearances. In mid-June, he also went on the IL with a right hamstring issue and was sidelined for approximately three weeks. However, Grisham told reporters that this strain was in a different spot, according to The Athletic's Chris Kirschner .

Jones will likely stay in center field for the Yankees' remaining 21 regular-season games. He's played 24 of his 61 games at that position with 16 starts. In 152 innings, advanced metrics rate him as slightly below average with -1 Defensive Runs Saved and -1 Outs Above Average. During his four-plus seasons in the minor leagues, Jones played 325 games in center.

Heliot Ramos played right field in Friday's game after Jones moved to center and he's starting there on Saturday. Ramos was picked up at the MLB trade deadline from the San Francisco Giants.

Jasson Domínguez was recalled from Triple-A Scranton/Wilkes-Barre to take Grisham's spot on the Yankees roster and he could play some right field, as well. He's played 41 games there during his time with the Yankees this season. In 53 major-league games, his slash line is .230/.270/.380, while he's slashing .283/.361/.420 in the minors.

Aaron Judge to face live pitching on Monday

However, Domínguez might not be on the Yankees' roster for long if Aaron Judge is activated from the injured list. The three-time American League MVP took on-field batting practice on Friday for the first time since suffering a stress fracture in his right rib cage.

Judge also ran the bases and worked in the outfield, indicating that he could return soon. Yankees manager Aaron Boone said Judge could be activated during the team's upcoming homestand from Sept. 8-13.

The Yankees slugger said he does not want to go on a minor-league rehab assignment and Boone said he will face live pitching on Monday. In lieu of a rehab assignment, Judge may initially play partial games when he returns.

articles.title: Cardinals Support Rincon With Tilted Hats in Photos, Rockies' Goodman Denies Complaining to Ump
articles.summary: Several St. Louis Cardinals players wore their hats tilted to the side as a show of support for rookie pitcher Hancel Rincon ahead of a matchup with the Colorado Rockies on Saturday.
articles.body:
Several St. Louis Cardinals players wore their hats tilted to the side as a show of support for rookie pitcher Hancel Rincon ahead of a matchup with the Colorado Rockies on Saturday.

On Friday, home plate umpire Doug Eddings called time to speak to Rincon about straightening his tilted hat in a clash with Colorado. Cardinals manager Oliver Marmol then argued with Eddings about the situation before he was later ejected .

During the verbal altercation between Marmol and Eddings, a pitch clock violation was given to Cardinals reliever Justin Bruihl.

Marmol said that he thought Eddings' actions were "embarrassing" after the game, as Rincon was making his MLB debut.

"Quite honestly, I thought it was pretty embarrassing on his end," Marmol told reporters . "We have a kid making his debut, and in-between an at-bat, he tells him he needs to fix the hat, and 'The kid's not going to wear his hat like that on my field.' Last I checked, this is Coors Field."

"So, I took issues with it," he added. "And the pitch violation while I'm out there having the discussion, that's also stupid, in my opinion... at the end of the day, I thought they handled it poorly, and I'd like an explanation at some point."

According to Derrick Goold of the St. Louis Post-Dispatch , Eddings said that the hat tilt was an "unwritten rule" and a Colorado batter pointed out the angle of Rincon's cap before he noticed it.

Rockies catcher Hunter Goodman, who faced Rincon to start the same inning in which the incident occurred, denied complaining about the right-hander's tilted hat.

"I never once mentioned the hat," Goodman said Saturday, per MLB.com's Thomas Harding . "It doesn't matter who's pitching. I don't care how they wear the hat. I'm trying to find out where the ball is coming out, and I'm trying to worry about what I'm doing in the box. I'm not worried about how his hat looks.

"It was one of those situations -- it's kind of a wild, wild thing that happens in the game. But I didn't like seeing that my name was a part of it today when I didn't say anything like that. You watch baseball growing up. There are a lot of guys who have had their hat crooked or however. Honestly, before today, when I went back and looked, I didn't even notice the hat was messed up or looked like that when I was hitting. Anyways, I don't pay attention to that stuff."

As the Cardinals continued their three-game series against the Rockies on Saturday, Rincon's teammates stood behind him.

Shelby Miller pitched on back-to-back nights for the first time in his rehab and got the loss. Miller was charged with four runs on two hits and two walks over two-thirds of an inning. He struck out two. However . . .

I should also mention that two of the runs charged to Miller scored after he left the game.

Left fielder Chas McCormick hit a solo home run in the second inning, his 13th on the season. McCormick was a perfect 3 for 3 before he left in the eighth inning after getting hit by a pitch.

Third baseman Owen Miller was 2 for 5 with one run driven in and one run scored.

Center fielder Justin Dean was 2 for 3 with a walk and a stolen base. He scored twice.

Dawson Netz and Tyler Schlaffer combined on a three-hit shutout. Netz pitched five innings and got the win after allowing just two hits. He struck out nine and walked two.

Schlaffer finished the game with the four-inning save. Schlaffer allowed just one hit and two walks while striking out seven.

So yeah, the Smokies two pitchers combined for 16 strikeouts.

Right fielder Alex Ramírez went 3 for 4 with a two-run double in the fourth.

Left fielder Carter Trice hit an RBI double in the eighth inning. Then he stole third base and scored on a bad throw. Trice went 1 for 4.

First baseman Miguel Useche was 2 for 4.

Dominick Reid was strong in his High-A debut, giving South Bend four scoreless innings on two hits. Reid struck out four and did not walk anyone.

The win went to Pierce Coppola in relief. Coppola gave up a run in the eighth and a run in the ninth. His final line was two runs on seven hits over 3.2 innings. Coppola struck out two and walked no one, but he did hit two batters.

JP Wheat was summoned from the pen to get South Bend's final out and pick up the save. Wheat faced two batters. He hit the first one and struck out the second, which sounds like a perfect Wheat outing.

Shortstop Angel Cepeda went 2 for 3 with a walk. He drove in one run and scored one run.

Center fielder Alexey Lumpuy was 2 for 3 with a bases-loaded walk and three steals. Lumpuy scored twice.

Right fielder Michael Gupton went 2 for 4 with a leadoff triple in the fifth inning. He was stranded there, but scored later on Lumpuy's bases-loaded walk.

Second baseman Jose Escobar went 2 for 3 with an RBI double and a sacrifice fly for two total RBI.

Lumpuy made a great catch in center field.

Rained out. As the season ends tomorrow and the game has no impact on playoff spots, it will not be made up.

articles.title: MLB Teams Next in Line for a New Stadium Amid Angels Rumors
articles.summary: Major League Baseball is overdue for a run on new stadiums.
articles.body:
Major League Baseball is overdue for a run on new stadiums.

If it felt like there was a new one every year for a while there, that's not totally wrong. Of the 30 active ballparks in the league today, 23 opened between 1989 and 2012. Since then, only Truist Park in Atlanta and Globe Life Field in Arlington have been added to the mix.

Times are changing, though. One club is actively building a new stadium, while another recently secured government approval for one. Several others are pursuing or teasing new stadiums, including the Los Angeles Angels following this week's $4 billion sale to Stan Kroenke.

It's clearly a good time to get a lay of the land ahead, so let's break down all the teams and cities that are next in line for a new stadium.

As of now, the Athletics' new stadium in Las Vegas is the only one that is for real happening.

In May, Mick Akers of the Las Vegas Review-Journal reported that the A's had spent $400 million out of their $2 billion allotment for the stadium, making it on time and on budget. It'll be right on the Las Vegas Strip on the corner of corner of Las Vegas Boulevard and Tropicana Avenue.

The stadium is only going to seat 33,000 fans, but a more intimate experience is the whole idea. They say that 80 percent of the seats are going to be within the foul poles, allowing for a shared view of the field with the Las Vegas skyline beyond the outfield.

The A's were a big draw in Oakland in the late 1980s and early 1990s, but less so as consistently low payrolls and gnarly conditions at the Oakland Coliseum drove fans away in the 2000s, 2010s and early 2020s. Naturally, they aren't drawing better in Sacramento since arriving last season. The only way to go from here is up.

At the same time, there has never seemed to be much demand for an MLB franchise in Las Vegas, and the A's brand doesn't exactly have the drawing power of, say, the Yankees, Dodgers, Red Sox or Cubs.

The NFL's Raiders have proved that a team can move from Oakland and find good attendance in Las Vegas, yet that has a lot to do with away fans coming to Las Vegas for a weekend. That kind of phenomenon may not translate to a 162-game baseball season that unfolds on a daily basis over six months.

This is hot off the presses, as a financing agreement for the Rays to build a new $2.3 billion stadium was only just approved last week .

The plan is to build it near Raymond James Stadium, which is about a half hour away from where the Rays currently call home at Tropicana Field. It's meant to be a stadium with at least 28,000 seats, indicating that, like the A's, the Rays are going for a more intimate feel.

Renderings for the new stadium make it look like a Mirror Universe version of Tropicana Field. Rather than dark and closed off, it looks intended to be bright and with a view of downtown Tampa beyond the outfield.

The Rays certainly hope the answer is yes. In fact, they're counting on it.

According to Marc Topkin of the Tampa Bay Times , majority owner Patrick Zalupski is already hyping up the Rays being able to afford top-15, maybe even top-10 payrolls upon moving into their new ballpark. The Rays are usually in the bottom five of the league in payroll.

Time could actually prove Zalupski to be wise. Though the Rays have never drawn well, they're not abandoning a fanbase like the A's did. And unlike Tropicana Field, the new site will actually be in the more populous Tampa instead of the less populous St. Petersburg.

This project isn't moving forward yet, but it's another where the latest development happened recently.

In late August, the Kansas City city council approved a $600 million commitment for a new stadium that would be part of a mixed-use development near downtown Kansas City. The team is footing another $760 million, with hopes that the state will provide an additional $540 million. The goal is to break ground in 2027.

It's unclear what the capacity is meant to be, but renderings released by the team depict the new stadium as a more modern-looking Kauffman Stadium. Most notably, there will still be fountains beyond the center field wall.

In all fairness, it's not as if the Royals currently play in fan-repellent stadium akin to the ones the A's and Rays are looking to leave behind. Kauffman Stadium generally rates highly, including among Yelp reviewers .

Nonetheless, Kauffman Stadium opened in 1973 and is thus firmly on the dated side. It also hasn't exactly been a place to be in recent years, with the Royals ranking in the bottom five of the AL in attendance annually since 2022.

Simply changing the location of where the Royals play home games could help bump the numbers up. Kauffman Stadium is not in downtown Kansas City, whereas the new site would be much closer in the Crown Center area.

MLB Fans Assemble Giant Hot Dog in Stands ▶️

The prospect of the White Sox building a new stadium in the proposed "The 78" neighborhood of Chicago first popped up in 2024, but it was a dream at that point as much as anything else. Plenty of renderings . No solid plan.

Now the ball is moving in the right direction, courtesy of future White Sox owner ( it's complicated ) Justin Ishbia.

As reported by Jon Greenberg of The Athletic on Saturday, Canal Edge, a development company controlled by Ishbia, announced plans for a new mixed-use development in the South Loop with a new White Sox stadium as its centerpiece. The proposed site is next to the Chicago River and is meant to be "integrated into the surrounding neighborhood fabric, with programmable open space, retail, and dining designed to activate the area 365 days a year."

Anything would be an upgrade over Rate Field. It opened in 1991, the year before Oriole Park at Camden Yards kicked off a wave of retro stadiums that felt like destinations as much as ballparks. The White Sox missed the boat.

If the White Sox do get a stadium at Ishbia's proposed site, there would be at least one major advantage beyond the newness of it all. The South Loop neighborhood is closer to the heart of Chicago, potentially making the new home of the White Sox a hot spot with greater access to more people.

The interesting thing is that the new site would move the White Sox closer to Wrigley Field. That potentially sets up a sort of turf war between the White Sox and Cubs for fans, which would heighten an already intense local rivalry.

Don't read too much into recent headlines boldly proclaiming that the Angels' owner-in-waiting, Stan Kroenke, already has plans to build a new stadium.

Those headlines stem from a report from Barry M. Bloom of Forbes that was subsequently corrected like so: "Information about building a new ballpark was removed from this story on Wednesday because a spokesperson for Kroenke said the Angels were not ready to move forward on the project at this time, but might in the future."

Still, this will do for a hint that Kroenke has a new stadium on his mind. It's definitely time for one, as Angel Stadium is 60 years old and not especially beloved.

Even sans solid plans for a new stadium, it already feels like a given that things are looking up for the Angels franchise.

Whereas Arte Moreno was a truly singular disaster as an owner, Kroenke's teams in the NFL, NBA and NHL have won championships. Once he's able to remake the franchise in his image, the Angels should go from being a perennial embarrassment to regular contenders.

As is, the franchise has the benefit of MLB's second-biggest market and the fifth-best attendance among AL clubs even amid one of the worst years in club history. Give this fanbase a new stadium, and the numbers can only go up.

Fair to Ask: Diamondbacks, Guardians, Blue Jays

As recently as 2022, Diamondbacks owner Ken Kendrick was openly musing about the possibility of a new stadium in the Phoenix area. Chase Field isn't that old, but it does feel dated and is not particularly well liked.

As of 2025, the D-backs are nonetheless supposed to remain at Chase Field for another 30 years after Arizona governor Katie Hobbs signed a bill that appropriates $500 million for renovations. Yet as Zach Buchanan of Axios reported, negotiations over the actual lease have grown contentious since then.

Stadium Status: Progressive Field since 1994

The Guardians have already gone the renovations route with Progressive Field, unveiling new improvements in 2024 and 2025. Those have helped modernize a ballpark that started as retro and was beginning to feel more like just plain old.

Yet since Progressive Field is MLB's 10th-oldest stadium, the relative oldness is still a thing. Maybe it won't happen soon, but the Guardians belong on list of teams to eye for a new stadium after the A's, Rays, Royals, White Sox and Angels get theirs.

Stadium Status: Rogers Centre since 1989

Like the Guardians, the Blue Jays have taken to renovating the Rogers Centre. It was a $400 million project undertaken between 2022 and 2024, and the stadium's aesthetics and general vibe are definitely better for it.

Yet as Blue Jays president Mark Shapiro said in 2022, the Rogers Centre renovations are "a medium-term solution." Rogers Centre is the sixth-oldest stadium in MLB, so it should just be a matter of time before concrete plans for a new ballpark are drawn up.

MLB commissioner Rob Manfred has talked a lot about expansion in recent years, and Maury Brown of Forbes recently cited three cities that "may currently have a bit of a leg up compared to the competition." Nashville is one of them. There is an organized effort to bring an MLB team, as well as a solid idea for a new stadium .

Salt Lake City is another of the three cities that may have an edge on other possible expansion sites. There's already a proposal for a $1.8 billion stadium and, just this past week, Shreyas Laddha of The Salt Lake Tribune reported on how Utah's bid for an MLB team "has only gained momentum."

Portland is the third city that may be ahead of all the others in pushing for an expansion team. In 2025, Oregon governor Tina Kotek signed a bill that authorizes up to $800 million for a new stadium. There are renderings for what it would look like on a piece of riverfront property on the Willamette River.

Orlando is a booming market, and it was even floated as a possible alternative for the Rays before they secured a deal for a new stadium in Tampa. The "Orlando Dreamers" project reportedly has $1.5 billion committed to team ownership and another $1 billion for a new stadium.

The Montreal Expos still live on social media , and there is a movement to bring them back . Baseball in Montreal famously did not work out the first time, but perhaps it's time to try again. The area has 4.4 million people living in it, and Olympic Stadium is still there and undergoing major renovations .

articles.title: Watch MLB Fans Put Giant Flying Hot Dog Into Giant Bun in Trending Video from Royals vs. Blue Jays
articles.summary: The Kansas City Royals may be having a season to forget, but their fans are certainly still having fun.
articles.body:
The Kansas City Royals may be having a season to forget, but their fans are certainly still having fun.

And how could they not when they successfully put a giant flying hot dog in a bun during Saturday's game against the Toronto Blue Jays:

Kansas City fans at Kauffman Stadium were separately bouncing around a large bun and large hot dog like beach balls at Kauffman Stadium on Saturday when they decided to bring them together. The crowd reacted with immediate joy upon the successful completion of the task, which was caught on video.

It also provided the fans more joy than the Royals, who lost 4-3 and fell to 63-80 as the last-place team in the American League Central.

articles.title: Shohei Ohtani Injury Return Timeline Updated by Dodgers Manager After IL Comments
articles.summary: There aren't many downsides to having a two-way star who hits and pitches like Shohei Ohtani on your roster, but the Los Angeles Dodgers could be facing one with the four-time MVP set to miss his fourth straight game with left knee and right biceps discomfort.
articles.body:
There aren't many downsides to having a two-way star who hits and pitches like Shohei Ohtani on your roster, but the Los Angeles Dodgers could be facing one with the four-time MVP set to miss his fourth straight game with left knee and right biceps discomfort.

Dodgers manager Dave Roberts said on Sunday that "if nothing else changes," he anticipates Ohtani playing on Monday against the Cincinnati Reds.

Since Ohtani is designated as a two-way player, he would have to go on the injured list for a minimum of 15 days instead of 10.

"That'd be more of a deterrent," Roberts said Saturday of potentially placing him on the IL, per Doug Padilla of the Associated Press.

While Roberts seemed optimistic that his star would return to the lineup soon, he downplayed the possibility of Ohtani pitching again this season.

Los Angeles could backdate the IL stint a maximum of three days if it does decide to make that move, but it would still be a significant amount of time without one of the best players in the league.

There was some progress, though, as Padilla noted Roberts said Ohtani took swings in the batting cages Saturday after not doing so the previous two days and did not report feeling discomfort.

"I feel that it's gotten a lot better given his demeanor the last couple days," Roberts said. "What I have learned about Shohei is when he doesn't feel well, physically, he gets more short, and it's just not the same personality, which makes sense. And so I think the last couple days he's gotten a lot more loose and easygoing."

Ohtani has not pitched since July 3 as the Dodgers manage his health and has struggled of late hitting just .137 with one home run in his last 13 games. Chicago Cubs star Pete Crow-Armstrong has seized control of the National League MVP race in the meantime with Ohtani not pitching or hitting like himself.

Still, the Dodgers will surely need the six-time All-Star back and healthy if they are going to win a third straight World Series title.

While a starting rotation that features Tarik Skubal, Yoshinobu Yamamoto, Blake Snell and Tyler Glasnow gives them plenty of remaining starpower on the mound, Ohtani is an elite hitter who can carry the offense throughout October.

He launched eight home runs in 17 postseason games last year and took home the National League Championship Series MVP in the win over the Milwaukee Brewers.

It remains to be seen whether the Dodgers will place Ohtani on the 15-day injured list, but they have a commanding 10.5-game lead in the National League West and will need him ready to go come playoff time as they look to remain atop the sport's mountaintop.

articles.title: Umpire Doug Eddings apologizes to Cardinals pitcher Hansel Rincon for telling him to straighten crooked cap
articles.summary: Eddings stopped play in the middle of an at-bat during Friday's game to tell the rookie hurler to fix his tilted cap.
articles.body:
Umpire Doug Eddings apologized to St. Louis Cardinals pitcher Hancel Rincon on Saturday for telling the rookie to straighten his tilted cap during Friday's 7-6 win over the Colorado Rockies.

Eddings' directive to Rincon caused an uproar that resulted in Cardinals manager Oliver Marmol being ejected from the game for arguing over what occurred.

"He apologized for what happened [Friday] night," Rincon said through bullpen catcher and team interpreter Kleininger Teran, via the St. Louis Post Dispatch's Derrick Goold . "He also told me good luck for the rest of my career as a big-leaguer."

The rookie added that he told Eddings, "'Don't worry, it's nothing personal, and everything stays here," according to MLB.com's Owen Perkins .

The incident in question occurred during the sixth inning of Friday's game as Rincon made his major-league debut. As the rookie was pitching to Colorado's Cole Carrigg, Eddings called timeout and appeared to tell Rincon (through Cardinals catcher Leo Bernal) to straighten the brim of his cap.

Rincon had already given up a triple to TJ Rumfield and thrown a wild pitch that allowed the Rockies first baseman to score. Following Eddings' stoppage, the right-hander then threw a 96 mph fastball right down the middle of the strike zone that Carrigg hit off the wall in right-center field for an eventual inside-the-park home run .

After that, Rincon allowed a single to Connor Norby and he was replaced by Justin Bruihl. He finished with three runs and three hits allowed in 1/3 of an inning. As Bruihl warmed up, Marmol came out to argue with Eddings and was ejected from the game.

Following the game, Eddings told reporters that Rockies catcher Hunter Goodman raised the issue of Rincon's cap , asking if it could be worn that way. The umpire acknowledged that Rincon was not breaking any MLB rule . However, Goodman denied saying anything.

"I never once mentioned the hat," Goodman said, via MLB.com's Thomas Harding . "It doesn't matter who's pitching. I don't care how they wear the hat. I'm trying to find out where the ball is coming out, and I'm trying to worry about what I'm doing in the box. I'm not worried about how his hat looks."

Before Saturday's game, which St. Louis lost 10-7 , Eddings talked to Marmol and Rockies manager Warren Schaeffer, then made sure to speak with Rincon as the Cardinals pitchers walked to the bullpen.

During batting practice, most of the Cardinals players wore their caps with the brim turned to the left in protest. Many of them continued to wear their caps crooked, as did several Rockies players, during the game. Several Cardinals fans behind home plate and radio broadcaster John Rooney also wore their caps with a crooked brim in solidarity.

"I felt big support from my teammates," Rincon said . "Obviously, when you are together, like this group, we're gonna be much better."

Rincon also pitched in Saturday's game, allowing four runs and two hits in one inning. In addition to inspiring a fashion statement during his brief MLB career, the rookie has compiled a 47.25 ERA in his two outings.

articles.title: Max Kepler DFA'd by D-Backs, Top Potential Landing Spots for MLB Playoff Races
articles.summary: The Arizona Diamondbacks announced Sunday they designated veteran outfielder Max Kepler for assignment.
articles.body:
The Arizona Diamondbacks announced Sunday they designated veteran outfielder Max Kepler for assignment.

The 33-year-old missed the first half of the 2026 MLB season through suspension and signed with Arizona in early June. He struggled mightily out west, putting up a .205/.262/.303 slash line in 41 appearances.

It's reasonable to conclude Kepler's suspension has impacted his performance, but he wasn't exactly lighting it up in previous years. Just once since 2020 has he finished with an OPS+ higher than 100, which represents the league average, per Baseball Reference .

With Sunday's move, another team will have the opportunity to add Kepler for the stretch run.

The Chicago White Sox could be one option after they just announced they placed Tommy Pham on the 10-day injured list.

The San Diego Padres make theoretical sense given their lack of depth and paucity of options on the left side of the plate. They took a flier on Austin Hays despite him having a .576 OPS with the White Sox, and signing Kepler wouldn't be any different from that.

The Boston Red Sox are in a similar bind. Masataka Yoshida remains sidelined with a hamstring injury , and they have no left-handers they can bring off the bench for a platoon advantage.

Granted, the hitting splits don't help Kepler's case for being a late-season signing. He's slugging just .283 against right-handed pitching and has struck out more times (29) than he got hits (23).

Unsung heroes always emerge around this time of the year. In the case of Kepler, it's hard to find any evidence supporting the idea he'll improve with a change of scenery.

Should he want to continue his career, he may have to wait until next spring to get his next MLB chance.

articles.title: Cardinals make decision on rookie pitcher days after Doug Eddings incident
articles.summary: St. Louis Cardinals right-handed pitcher Hancel Rincon had an incident with umpire Doug Eddings on Friday.
articles.body:
As rosters expanded to 28 players on Tuesday, the St. Louis Cardinals used one of their extra spots to call up right-handed pitcher Hancel Rincon from Triple-A Memphis. The 24-year-old made his MLB debut Friday.

In that game against the Colorado Rockies, Rincon entered the game to start the bottom of the sixth inning. He had already faced two batters and got into a 2-0 count on a third when umpire Doug Eddings told him to adjust his hat.

Rincon was wearing it off to the side, and after complying with Eddings' demand, allowed an inside-the-park home run to Rockies center fielder Cole Carrigg.

Rincon faced four batters in total before being lifted from the game. Cardinals manager Oli Marmol was frustrated with Eddings since the hat incident a few minutes prior, and was ejected following the pitching change.

Sep 4, 2026; Denver, Colorado, USA; St. Louis Cardinals manager Oliver Marmol (37) argues with home plate umpire Doug Eddings (88) in the sixth inning against the Colorado Rockies at Coors Field. Mandatory Credit: Isaiah J. Downing-Imagn Images Credit: IMAGN IMAGES via Reuters Connect (Reuters)

The next day, St. Louis players wore their hats to the side in protest. According to their broadcast, some Colorado players did as well. Eddings apologized to Rincon for his actions from the previous night before the game.

The 24-year-old got into Saturday's game, throwing the sixth inning again. He allowed four runs on two hits and a walk while picking up his first MLB strikeout. Overall, Rincon had a rocky weekend in Denver. He surrendered seven earned runs in 1 ⅓ innings pitched, walking one and striking out one.

The scuffle with Eddings happened close to the start of his Friday appearance, which might have impacted his performance. Ahead of Sunday's game, Rincon was demoted to Triple-A with lefty long man Cooper Hjerpe coming up to MLB.

The 25-year-old was taken in the first round of the 2022 draft by the Cardinals, but has struggled with injury during his minor league career. He sat out all of 2025 with Tommy John Surgery, but has pitched well since his return earlier this season.

In five starts and 19 innings at Memphis, Hjerpe has pitched to a 0.95 ERA, striking out 27 and walking 17. He has always been a high-strikeout high-walk guy, but these numbers do jump off the page.

Pitchers usually struggle with command after coming back from TJ, so hopefully that is all it is. He will now be working with an MLB staff as the Cardinals (70-70) attempt to make a run for the third National League Wild Card spot.

articles.title: Umpire Doug Eddings apologizes to Cardinals pitcher Hansel Rincon after MLB reportedly reprimanded him for telling rookie to straighten crooked cap
articles.summary: Eddings stopped play in the middle of an at-bat during Friday's game to tell the rookie hurler to fix his tilted cap.
articles.body:
Umpire Doug Eddings apologized to St. Louis Cardinals pitcher Hancel Rincon on Saturday for telling the rookie to straighten his tilted cap during Friday's 7-6 win over the Colorado Rockies.

However, the veteran umpire reportedly felt compelled to do so after Major League Baseball told him that he acted inappropriately in admonishing Rincon, according to The Athletic's Ken Rosenthal .

Eddings' directive to Rincon caused an uproar that resulted in Cardinals manager Oliver Marmol being ejected from the game for arguing over what occurred.

"He apologized for what happened [Friday] night," Rincon said through bullpen catcher and team interpreter Kleininger Teran, via the St. Louis Post Dispatch's Derrick Goold . "He also told me good luck for the rest of my career as a big-leaguer."

The rookie added that he told Eddings, "'Don't worry, it's nothing personal, and everything stays here," according to MLB.com's Owen Perkins .

The incident in question occurred during the sixth inning of Friday's game as Rincon made his major-league debut. As the rookie was pitching to Colorado's Cole Carrigg, Eddings called timeout and appeared to tell Rincon (through Cardinals catcher Leo Bernal) to straighten the brim of his cap.

Rincon had already given up a triple to TJ Rumfield and thrown a wild pitch that allowed the Rockies first baseman to score. Following Eddings' stoppage, the right-hander then threw a 96 mph fastball right down the middle of the strike zone that Carrigg hit off the wall in right-center field for an eventual inside-the-park home run .

After that, Rincon allowed a single to Connor Norby and he was replaced by Justin Bruihl. He finished with three runs and three hits allowed in 1/3 of an inning. As Bruihl warmed up, Marmol came out to argue with Eddings and was ejected from the game.

Following the game, Eddings told reporters that Rockies catcher Hunter Goodman raised the issue of Rincon's cap , asking if it could be worn that way. The umpire acknowledged that Rincon was not breaking any MLB rule . However, Goodman denied saying anything.

"I never once mentioned the hat," Goodman said, via MLB.com's Thomas Harding . "It doesn't matter who's pitching. I don't care how they wear the hat. I'm trying to find out where the ball is coming out, and I'm trying to worry about what I'm doing in the box. I'm not worried about how his hat looks."

Before Saturday's game, which St. Louis lost 10-7 , Eddings talked to Marmol and Rockies manager Warren Schaeffer, then made sure to speak with Rincon as the Cardinals pitchers walked to the bullpen. This reportedly occurred after MLB told Eddings that he went too far by telling Rincon to straighten his cap.

It's uncertain whether or not Eddings could be disciplined further by MLB for the incident, Rosenthal reports.

During batting practice, most of the Cardinals players wore their caps with the brim turned to the left in protest. Many of them continued to wear their caps crooked, as did several Rockies players, during the game. Several Cardinals fans behind home plate and radio broadcaster John Rooney also wore their caps with a crooked brim in solidarity.

"I felt big support from my teammates," Rincon said . "Obviously, when you are together, like this group, we're gonna be much better."

Rincon also pitched in Saturday's game, allowing four runs and two hits in one inning. In addition to inspiring a fashion statement during his brief MLB career, the rookie has compiled a 47.25 ERA in his two outings.

articles.title: MLB Says Umpire Went 'Too Far' with Cardinals Ejection, Rincon's Tilted Hat in New Rumors
articles.summary: Major League Baseball alerted umpire Doug Eddings he crossed a line by instructing St. Louis Cardinals pitcher Hancel Rincón to straighten his hat and ejecting Cardinals manager Oli Marmol in the team's 7-6 win over the Colorado Rockies on Friday.
articles.body:
Major League Baseball alerted umpire Doug Eddings he crossed a line by instructing St. Louis Cardinals pitcher Hancel Rincón to straighten his hat and ejecting Cardinals manager Oli Marmol in the team's 7-6 win over the Colorado Rockies on Friday.

"Umpires operate with broad discretion if they believe a player's actions are distracting, but according to two people briefed on the matter who were granted anonymity because they are not authorized to speak publicly, the league viewed Eddings' admonishment of Rincon as going too far," Ken Rosenthal of The Athletic reported.

Midway through the sixth inning, Eddings called time and motioned for Rincón to straighten his hat. The rookie reliever had turned his bill slightly to the left, a style that some MLB players wear.

Marmol replaced Rincón later in the inning for Justin Bruihl. He and Eddings had a discussion as Bruihl was warming up. After the manager returned to the dugout, Eddings called a pitch clock violation, and Marmol's renewed complaints eventually resulted in his ejection.

Fans immediately questioned why Eddings made a point to address Rincón's hat when it's relatively commonplace in MLB. Hall of Famer CC Sabathia and three-time All-Star Fernando Rodney both made it one of their signatures, and neither faced any issues.

Marmol described the umpire's actions as "power-hungry."

The scrutiny on Eddings grew when he claimed Rockies catcher Hunter Goodman suggested to him that Rincón should straighten his hat. Goodman denied the assertion.

"I never once mentioned the hat," Goodman said Saturday, per MLB.com's Thomas Harding . "It doesn't matter who's pitching. I don't care how they wear the hat. I'm trying to find out where the ball is coming out, and I'm trying to worry about what I'm doing in the box. I'm not worried about how his hat looks."

In a show of solidarity, Cardinals players and some from Colorado tilted their hats during Saturday's contest.

It appears Eddings attempted to apologize to Rincón, but Rincón said he only "understood a couple words" as the conversation unfolded on the field without an interpreter.

Rosenthal relayed a statement from an MLB spokesperson.

"Saturday's gesture of apology by Doug on the field speaks for itself," they said.

Rosenthal added that it's unknown whether MLB will issue any discipline to Eddings.

Rincón is no longer on the Cardinals' active roster after St. Louis optioned him to Triple-A on Sunday.

articles.title: Aaron Judge, Trent Grisham Injury Updates Discussed by Yankees' Aaron Boone
articles.summary: New York Yankees manager Aaron Boone still isn't committing to naming a return date for star Aaron Judge.
articles.body:
New York Yankees manager Aaron Boone still isn't committing to naming a return date for star Aaron Judge.

When asked whether Judge could be back on the field on Tuesday, Boone was noncommittal.

"I don't know," he told reporters . "We'll see."

Judge was also vague, saying that he'll make his return "hopefully soon."

Boone did offer an update on Trent Grisham, saying that the center fielder has a Grade 2 right hamstring sprain and could miss the rest of the regular season.

Judge has been out since late May with a fractured rib but appears to be trending towards a return as the postseason nears.

Boone told reporters on Saturday that Judge would face live pitchers on Monday, his first time doing so since landing on the injured list. He previously took batting practice swings on Friday, another step in his rehab.

"I'm mad how long it has taken," Judge said on Friday. "It is what it is. I wish it was real two months ago, but we're at this point [now]. We're getting close. I can't wait to be back out there."

Judge, who also ran the bases and did fielding work on Friday, added that facing live pitchers might be the last step in getting back on the field.

"We're hitting all the baseball stuff," Judge said. "Throwing to bases, throwing, running the bases. Hitting, getting on the field, moving around. I think [we need to] face some live pitching and then I'll get back out there. ... We're trying to get the volume up so that we can be in a good spot. Because not doing nothing for three months, man, it feels like an offseason and you're kind of going back into Spring Training."

Before his injury, Judge was hitting .248 with 17 homers, 38 RBI, 43 runs and a .907 OPS across 59 games. While his numbers were slightly down by his standards, the Yankees' lineup has certainly taken a hit without him.

Still, New York has managed to stay afloat without Judge and is currently sitting in second place in the AL East at 81-61. The Yankees are also 9.5 games ahead in the wild-card race.

While Judge may be trending towards a return, losing Grisham for the remainder of the season would be another blow. He's hitting .211 this year with 18 home runs and 59 RBI, so the Yankees would lose a bit of pop at the plate.

The end of the MLB regular season is just weeks away, and teams are fighting hard to secure their postseason spot.

Some teams are sitting comfortably at this point in the year, while others still have work to do. Here's a look at how things look heading into this week.

Yankees star pitcher on wrong side of history

Sunday was decisive for one team, as the Colorado Rockies became the first team to be eliminated from playoff contention after losing to the St. Louis Cardinals.

There isn't too much drama in the AL East as the Rays have just about secured the divisional crown. The Yankees and Red Sox are essentially locks to make the postseason, meaning the Blue Jays are the team to watch in the division. Toronto would need a strong finish to get back into the playoffs, but it's far from impossible.

The White Sox are likely postseason-bound but will need to continue fending off the Guardians for the AL Central title. Those two will face off next week in a series that could have plenty of implications.

The Astros have had a good stretch as of late that has helped them increase their lead in the AL West, though the Rangers aren't out of the race just yet, and the Mariners are technically within striking distance.

There's far less drama in the National League, where the Braves, Phillies, Brewers, Cubs and Dodgers have all virtually secured a postseason spot. The biggest race to watch is between the Arizona Diamondbacks and San Diego Padres for the final wild-card spot.

articles.title: Cubs Minor League Wrap: Knoxville knocks out Lookouts, 6-5
articles.summary: Justin Steele starts for Iowa. The regular season ends for South Bend and Myrtle Beach.
articles.body:
Labor Day is the traditional end of the Minor League season, but that's gone a bit by the wayside with the reorganization of the minors in 2021. However, Labor Day is late enough this year that the regular season ends today for South Bend and Myrtle Beach. However, South Bend's season will continue next week in the playoffs.

In his second rehab start with Iowa, Justin Steele pitched two innings and allowed one run on two hits. He struck out one and walked no one. Steele threw 27 pitches and 18 were strikes, so he was finding the strike zone. Steele's velocity on his four-seam fastball was 90-to-92 miles per hour.

Kohl Franklin then pitched the next two innings and got the loss after giving up a three-run home run to Kahlil Watson. Franklin's final line was three runs on two hits and walk. He struck out one.

Jaxon Wiggins pitched the ninth inning and coughed up a run on one hit and one walk. It was the first run Wiggins has allowed over nine relief appearances stretching over nine innings. He struck out one.

Left fielder Jordan Nwogu cranked a solo home run in the second inning and a sacrifice fly in the eighth for two total RBI. He was 1 for 3.

Right fielder Justin Dean doubled twice in a 2 for 4 game. He drove in one.

Third baseman James Triantos was 2 for 4.

As a Michigan Wolverine, Nwogu loves terrorizing Columbus.

Dean with an RBI double after the Guardians messed up a rundown.

For the first time in his career, Kevin Alcántara played first base. He was 0 for 4 at the plate though.

The Knoxville Smokies got in the eyes of the Chattanooga Lookouts (Reds), 6-5. The Smokies now have a two-game lead over both Rocket City and Birmingham with six games to play. Of course, it doesn't make any difference as the Smokies won the first half already, but it would be nice to win both halves.

Connor Schultz started and held the Lookouts to just one unearned run on four hits over four innings. Schultz struck out three and walked one.

Yenrri Rojas came on to pitch the seventh inning and retired the next nine batters in order and picked up the win because Schultz didn't go five. Rojas struck out one over those three innings.

First baseman Miguel Useche hit a two-run home run in the bottom of the first inning. It was his 13th of the season and sixth with Knoxville. Useche went 1 for 4.

Right fielder Alex Ramírez doubled the Smokies lead to 4-0 with a two-run home run in the second inning. Ramírez was 2 for 5. It was his 15th home run this year.

DH Andy Garriola homered with the bases empty in the third inning, his 22nd on the season. Garriola went 2 for 4.

Shortstop Alex Madera was 2 for 4 with an RBI double in the third inning.

Ramírez's home run looked like it touched the clouds.

The South Bend Cubs finished their regular season with a 10-5 loss to the Cedar Rapids Kernels (Twins).

Anhuar Garcia started and gave the Cubs three innings. He was touched for three runs on eight hits. Garcia struck out three and walked no one.

Luke Alwood took the loss after he gave up three unearned runs in the sixth inning, all coming after two were out. Right fielder Kade Snell dropped a shallow fly that would have ended the inning. I think Snell may have lost it in the sun, but he got his glove on it and it bounced right out. Alwood's final line was three unearned runs on one hit and three walks over 1.2 innings. He struck out two.

First baseman Josiah Hartshorn hit two doubles and walked once in a 2 for 4 game. Hartshorn drove in three runs and scored once. He finished the season with a South Bend Cubs record 85 RBI after his promotion and he had 110 total in 122 games.

Shortstop Angel Cepeda was 2 for 5 with an RBI double.

Second baseman Jose Escobar went 1 for 3 with a walk and an RBI single.

Josiah Hartshorn just keeps driving in runs.

South Bend finished the second half in third place with a 38-28 record after winning the first half. Their overall record was 77-51, which was the best record in the Midwest League.

South Bend will start the best-of-three playoffs on Tuesday in the Quad Cities against the River Bandits. Games 2 and 3, if necessary, will be in South Bend on Thursday and Friday.

The Pelicans season finale was rained out.

The Pelicans finished the second half with a record of 23-40, which puts them in last place in the Carolina League South Division. Their overall record was 50-77 which was again last in their division, but at least it was better than Delmarva, who finished in last in the North Division.

articles.summary: Former Louisville Bats pitcher Aroldis Chapman became the ninth player in MLB history to record 400 career saves.
articles.body:
Pat Kelsey celebrates bobblehead day at Louisville Slugger Field

Former Louisville Bats pitcher Aroldis Chapman recorded his 400th career Major League save Sunday in Boston's 3-1 win over the Baltimore Orioles .

Chapman, who started his pro career with the Bats in 2010, became the ninth pitcher in MLB history to reach 400 saves.

Chapman struck out Coby Mayo and Christian Encarnacion-Strand in the bottom of the ninth inning to capture the feat. The left handed pitcher has recorded 24 total saves against Baltimore.

This season, Chapman has recorded 33 saves, 65 strikeouts and a 2.03 ERA.

The Cincinnati Reds signed Chapman as a free agent in January 2010 and sent him to the Bats. He began as a starting pitcher before transitioning to the bullpen.

He went 9-6 with eight saves and 3.57 ERA in 39 appearances with the Bats before the Reds promoted him to Cincinnati for the playoff run. Chapman turned into four-time All-Star with the Reds before they traded him to the New York Yankees.

articles.title: Red Sox Closer Aroldis Chapman Discusses 'Special' Moment Reaching 400 Career Saves
articles.summary: Boston Red Sox closer Aroldis Chapman hit the 400-save mark on Sunday, preserving a 3-1 win over the Baltimore Orioles and a four-game sweep in the process.
articles.body:
Boston Red Sox closer Aroldis Chapman hit the 400-save mark on Sunday, preserving a 3-1 win over the Baltimore Orioles and a four-game sweep in the process.

He's just the ninth pitcher in MLB history to reach that milestone.

Yankees star pitcher on wrong side of history

"It's very special," Chapman told reporters about the accomplishment. "A few years back, I lost my role as a closer. When I came here they gave me an opportunity to compete for the job. I was able to win it. [Getting 400 saves] was one of the things I wanted to do in my career. There was a moment when I didn't think I would be able to do it."

Chapman, 38, is now 3-4 on the season with 33 saves, a 2.03 ERA, a 1.13 WHIP and 65 strikeouts in just 48.2 innings. He remains one of the best relievers in the sport, and now he's entered the illustrious 400-save club.

articles.title: Buy or Sell Each MLB Playoff Contender Advancing in 2026 Postseason
articles.summary: Ready or not, the 2026 Major League Baseball postseason is rapidly approaching.
articles.body:
Ready or not, the 2026 Major League Baseball postseason is rapidly approaching.

Will the Dodgers make it back to the World Series, possibly for a repeat of 2024 against the Yankees? Or could it be a drastically different budgetary battle between the Brewers and the Rays in which the victor secures its first-ever title?

Thus far, no one has clinched a playoff spot. However, both Milwaukee and Tampa Bay could do so this week, and there are 10 teams that look to be relatively locked into the 12-team field.

For the five teams currently behind that tier but still within three games of the cut line, our focus is on whether they'll make the postseason at all, buying or selling those odds, per FanDuel .

After that, we've listed each team's postseason odds—from making the playoffs through to winning the World Series—using percentages from Baseball-Reference and FanGraphs , as well as World Series betting lines from FanDuel.

Unless otherwise noted, all statistics, records and odds are current through the start of play on Sunday.

Teams are presented in alphabetical order.

ATL | BOS | CHC | CWS | HOU | LAD | MIL | NYY | PHI | TB

5 Teams Fighting for 2 Final Playoff Spots

There are 10 teams with at least an 88.8 percent chance of reaching the postseason, per the consensus of Baseball-Reference playoff odds, FanGraphs playoff odds and the implied odds of FanDuel's "To Reach the Playoffs" lines. Those 10 teams will get their own section speculating on their staying power in October.

These are the five teams on the cut line, still realistically vying for the final spot on their half of the bracket. Rather than project how far they might go in the postseason, we're focused more on whether they'll make it to October at all.

Arizona Diamondbacks (current No. 6 seed, 0.5 games ahead of San Diego; 55.5% postseason odds per FanGraphs/Baseball-Reference, -105 to make postseason via FanDuel)

San Diego Padres (0.5 games behind Arizona for No. 6 seed; 40.0% postseason odds per FanGraphs/Baseball-Reference, -105 to make postseason via FanDuel)

With Miami and St. Louis now four games back and Pittsburgh another game behind that duo, it's effectively down to Arizona and San Diego for the NL's No. 6 seed. And though it's possible the race could be decided before then, it's looking very likely that the Arizona at San Diego series for games 160-162 will be the difference-maker.

San Diego definitively was the better team in August, but Arizona is about to get a slightly ridiculous influx of pitching help. Corbin Burnes is expected to make his season debut on Tuesday against the Royals, while Zac Gallen, Michael Soroka and Ryne Nelson tentatively could return within the next week. That could be quite an upgrade after the Diamondbacks spent the past few weeks hoping for the best from rookies and openers.

Meanwhile, Joe Musgrove's return to San Diego was delayed yet again, and we're still waiting to hear if and when Nick Pivetta will be back.

The Padres had been my pick since the trade deadline, but things seem to be shifting in Arizona's favor. And if Burnes can even remotely look like his old self, the Diamondbacks could even be a spoiler in the postseason. At any rate, it wouldn't be the first time they made a run as the No. 6 seed.

Cleveland Guardians (tied with Toronto for No. 6 seed; 2.5 GB behind Chicago for AL Central lead; 41.1% postseason odds per FanGraphs/Baseball-Reference, +122 to make postseason via FanDuel)

Toronto Blue Jays (tied with Cleveland for No. 6 seed; 51.7% postseason odds per FanGraphs/Baseball-Reference, -120 to make postseason via FanDuel)

Texas Rangers (2.0 GB CLE/TOR; 3.0 GB Houston for AL West lead; 15.1% postseason odds per FanGraphs/Baseball-Reference, +370 to make postseason via FanDuel)

One of these things is not like the other, but Texas is one strong week away from catapulting into the mix, either as the No. 6 seed or the No. 3 seed. Considering the Rangers still have on their docket a three-game series at home against Toronto, they definitely aren't dead yet.

Here's the thing, though: That series against a Texas team that is three games below .500 is the toughest thing left on the Blue Jays schedule. They otherwise have six games against 69-74 Baltimore and three games apiece against 68-74 Cincinnati, 65-77 Detroit, 63-80 Kansas City and the 57-86 Athletics.

And whereas Seattle has completely muffed its gift from the schedule makers by losing three straight to the A's, Toronto has already been red hot at 23-12 in its last 35 games and now gets the benefit of clear skies ahead.

A repeat run to the World Series is pretty unlikely. Aside from Dylan Cease, the starting rotation is riddled with question marks, and we are forever waiting for Vladimir Guerrero Jr. to look like his old self at the plate. But they really ought to make the postseason.

(For what it's worth, Toronto holds the head-to-head tiebreaker over Cleveland.)

Reach NLDS / NLCS / World Series : 65.6% / 28.6% / 12.5%

At the end of play on June 7, Atlanta had the best record in the majors by a three-game margin.

Dating back to July 12, only the Red Sox (33-17) have had a better record than the Braves (30-18).

But things went so sideways for the five weeks in between (9-19) that a lot of people wrote Atlanta out of the World Series conversation; an also-ran compared to Milwaukee and Los Angeles.

If you were one of those folks, it's not too late to reconsider, now that the pitching staff is looking more formidable.

Thus far in the second half, Chris Sale has a 1.90 ERA with 67 strikeouts against just four walks. However, that's nothing new after he (and the bullpen) carried Atlanta through the first half.

The big question was whether anyone else would become a viable second fiddle behind that Cy Young hopeful in this rotation.

To that end, Tyler Mahle had a 1.48 ERA in his first five starts after Atlanta acquired him from San Francisco, and Martín Pérez opened the second half with a 2.04 ERA in his first eight starts.

Is it a flash in the pan, or can those two veterans carry that new-found dominance into the postseason?

If it's the latter, there's more than enough pop in this lineup for Atlanta to do some real damage in October.

Buy/Sell : Buying Atlanta at 28.6% to reach NLCS and at +1300 to win World Series

Reach ALDS / ALCS / World Series : 51.9% / 28.4% / 17.0%

For a while there, Boston was an unstoppable freight train and the clear pick to win the World Series. After starting out 32-46, the Red Sox went 32-5 from June 25 through August 7. Easily one of the most absurd in-season turnarounds in MLB history.

Because outside of Mickey Gasper becoming Mickey Mantle out of nowhere and Roman Anthony looking great in his return from nearly four months on the IL, the Red Sox have been low-key mid over the past month.

Adley Rutschman hasn't been the game-changer at catcher that they were hoping for. Shortstop remains a mess—while the Red Sox refuse to call up Franklin Arias to potentially address that problem. The pitching staff that had a 2.79 ERA during that 37-game stretch of dominance has had a 4.23 ERA (and a .500 record) since.

To make matters worse, it's starting to look like they are locked in as the No. 5 seed. That means needing to win a wild card series at Yankee Stadium in order to then run into a Tampa Bay team that has been unflappable at Tropicana Park this season. And that's just to reach the ALCS.

Unless late-June through early-August Boston shows up again, that's a tough ask.

Buy/Sell : Selling Red Sox at 28.4% to reach ALCS

Updated New York Yankees Playoff Predictions, Aaron Judge Projections

Reach NLDS / NLCS / World Series : 50.2% / 23.3% / 10.8%

Beyond a shadow of a doubt, the Cubs have the offensive firepower to make some real noise in October.

They are leading the majors in runs scored, as well as home runs hit, reaching 200 for the year in the latter department in Saturday's win over the Marlins. And though Pete Crow-Armstrong is the clear leader of the bunch as the NL MVP favorite, everybody 1 through 9 in this lineup can do some damage.

How much run support is this pitching staff going to need, though?

Chicago has averaged 6.3 runs per game over its last 26 contests, but it only has a 13-13 record to show for it, because it is also allowing nearly five runs per game.

That's even with midseason additions Kevin Gausman, Clay Holmes and David Peterson fully implemented into the rotation. But Holmes is the only starter in this rotation with an ERA better than 4.82 during that stretch.

The bullpen has also been a mess, with Jacob Webb losing what always was a tenuous grasp on the role of primary closer. It's now a revolving door of trying to play matchups, with Ryan Zeferjahn recently becoming the 14th different pitcher to record a save for the Cubs this season. And "closer by committee" situations rarely if ever work out for the best in October.

Got to like their chances in any short series. But winning a best-of-seven with this pitching staff—let alone two in a row—probably isn't happening.

Buy/Sell : Selling Chicago at +1700 to win World Series

Reach ALDS / ALCS / World Series : 71.8% / 32.5% / 15.3%

We'll say this much before we question Chicago's staying power: The projected path to the ALCS is quite nice. Time will tell if they can ultimately hold on to the AL's No. 2 seed, but getting a first-round bye before drawing the winner of Houston vs. Toronto/Cleveland is about as favorable as it gets.

This is also the American League's highest scoring team we're talking about. The big three of Munetaka Murakami, Colson Montgomery and Miguel Vargas could spearhead an offensive charge deep into October.

Does anyone realistically believe in this pitching staff, though?

In August alone, the White Sox used 10 different starting pitchers. The only one of the bunch to do so with a sub-4.29 ERA was Sean Newcomb—who made three scoreless appearances as an opener and almost certainly isn't going to be part of the postseason rotation.

Luis Castillo made one phenomenal start against the Reds, but has otherwise been a disaster with a 7.52 ERA since the White Sox traded for him.

As a result, Chicago allowed 140 runs in August, going 14-14 overall as they forever hover between three and nine games above .500.

It's an unbelievable story that they're (most likely) going to reach the postseason after three straight seasons of at least 100 losses. But it's probably not going to be an unforgettable October for the White Sox.

Buy/Sell : Selling White Sox at 32.5% to reach ALCS

Reach ALDS / ALCS / World Series : 59.8% / 29.3% / 12.5%

While Boston's recovery from a brutal start to the season seemed to happen in one fell swoop, Houston's revival has been much more of a slow burn, kind of quietly sitting at 14 games over .500 since reaching their lowest point in mid-May.

And, well, it's a slow burn because the starting rotation has been an unreliable mess with an ERA just a shade under 5.00 over the last 92 games.

Hayden Wesneski has given the Astros solid work since returning from Tommy John surgery in late July. Hunter Brown also has a sub-3.00 ERA over his last eight starts. But Peter Lambert has come crashing back to earth and no one else who they've deployed has even been passable.

We've gotten to the point where Houston's best option in a do-or-die Game 3 of the wild card round might be a bullpen game.

That having been said, their bullpen has been arguably the best in baseball over the past three months.

Josh Hader has a 0.69 ERA since making his season debut on June 3. And, for whatever reason, Hader's return was the shot in the arm that Bryan Abreu needed, boasting a 1.51 ERA compared to a 7.91 mark across his first 22 appearances. Steven Okert has also been quite the asset with 45 strikeouts against just four walks in his last 39 outings.

If they get a lead in the sixth inning or later, they probably aren't blowing it. And goodness knows the Astros have some guys who can hit in October, most notably Yordan Alvarez and Jose Altuve. They could at least make it an eighth ALCS appearance in the past decade, given their projected path of Toronto/Cleveland and Chicago. (There's still a good chance they secure a first-round bye, too, just 1.5 games behind the White Sox.)

Buy/Sell : Buying Astros at 29.3% to reach ALCS

Reach NLDS / NLCS / World Series : 91.9% / 54.3% / 32.4%

You probably noticed immediately that the betting line and the forecasting models aren't even remotely in agreement here.

The +175 line from FanDuel suggests a 36.4 percent chance of winning the World Series, while the consensus from FanGraphs and Baseball-Reference is that there's a 32.4 percent chance the Dodgers will even make the World Series.

And, well, at 28-26 since the beginning of July with a real possibility they won't even receive a first-round bye, we're inclined to agree with the forecasting models on this one.

Granted, we've seen this song and dance from the Dodgers before.

They went 25-27 between July and August of last season before finishing with a flourish (15-5 in final 20 games) and repeating as World Champs. They also sputtered to a 19-19 record from early July through mid-August in 2024, but went 26-12 over the final six weeks of the regular season.

If the light bulb suddenly comes on tomorrow and they go on a rampage fueled by a favorable schedule and one of the most stacked starting rotations in recent history, we won't exactly pretend to be shocked.

With Shohei Ohtani slumping at the dish (and injured), Kyle Tucker struggling all season long, Andy Pages on the shelf and a bullpen that simply hasn't been good since the All-Star break?

Buy/Sell : Selling Dodgers at +175 to win World Series

Reach NLDS / NLCS / World Series : 96.4% / 52.9% / 26.0%

Over the past few years, the Brewers have been the most consistently solid regular-season team. Since the beginning of 2023, they rank first in the majors in ERA, second in on-base percentage, second in total wins and fifth in total runs scored.

For some reason, though, that keeps going out the window in October, ranking dead-last in on-base percentage (.295), dead-last in scoring (3.0 R/G) and slightly worse than average in ERA (3.98) among the 12 teams who have played at least 12 games across the past three postseasons.

Scoring a grand total of four runs while getting swept out of last year's NLCS was the epitome of brutality for them, but it also wasn't a particularly new development for the thrice-reigning NL Central champions who are 5-16 overall in their past six playoff appearances.

Maybe this is the year it changes and they finally break through for their first World Series appearance since 1982?

But Kyle Harrison, Dustin May, Shane Drohan and Robert Gasser have all struggled in recent weeks, leaving all sorts of question marks about this postseason rotation—aside from Jacob Misiorowski, of course.

What's more, the fact that the Brewers have spent most of this season ranked dead last in the majors in home runs has been a growing concern about their staying power in October.

We want to believe in the team with the best record in baseball, but it also feels like Lucy Van Pelt is holding the football here.

Buy/Sell : Selling the Brewers at +650 to win World Series, but buying them at 52.9% chance of reaching NLCS

Reach ALDS / ALCS / World Series : 57.9% / 31.9% / 18.8%

There are two gigantic questions we'd love to have answered about the Yankees before making any proclamations about their October potential.

The first is whether they can overtake Tampa Bay to win the AL East.

The Yankees have been a wild card team 10 times in franchise history, and they failed to reach the World Series all 10 times. And this season in particular, the difference between being the No. 1 seed and the No. 4 seed feels massive.

The bigger question, though, is the status of Aaron Judge.

He hasn't played since May 31 and had a very un-Judge-like .550 OPS in his final 16 games before landing on the IL with the rib injury. But there's a non-zero chance he'll return this week, as well as a non-zero chance he quickly gets back to looking like the superstar who won three of the past four AL MVPs.

If that happens, New York might be able to get the coveted No. 1 seed, but could cruise through the AL half of the bracket either way.

The Yankees were averaging 5.2 runs per game with Judge compared to barely 4.0 without him. Yet, their pitching has been so good over the past two months that they've still been one of the better teams without him. Getting an infusion of his bat into the lineup would be huge.

For now, though, it looks like they're destined to face Boston in the wild card round. And, for now, it would be foolish to just assume Judge is going to return good as new. That one-two punch makes it tough to endorse the Yankees as the AL team most likely to win the World Series.

Buy/Sell : Selling Yankees at +850 to win World Series

Reach NLDS / NLCS / World Series : 52.4% / 25.0% / 12.3%

At 23-9 since the beginning of August, the Phillies have been the hottest team in baseball as of late.

For starters, their "other" starters have been on point. Andrew Painter entered August with a 6.72 ERA while Aaron Nola was at 5.61. The Phillies were a combined 12-25 when either one pitched. But they've been at 3.15 and 2.65, respectively, since then, with the Phillies going 8-4 in those games.

They've also gotten major contributions from hitters other than Bryce Harper and Kyle Schwarber. Alec Bohm has turned his season around, batting .330 over his last 30 games. Justin Crawford is also hitting nearly .300, as is Luis Arraez since they added him to the mix.

And that has been the X-factor with this team all season long: Who shows up aside from the main six stars?

When the supporting cast is making big contributions, the Phillies have a chance to do something special.

The problem, however, is that they're probably not going to win the NL East. As things currently stand, they would need to go through the Cubs, the Brewers and probably the Dodgers just to reach the World Series.

With as hot as they've been, that's plausible. But it's a tough ask.

Buy/Sell : Selling Philadelphia at +1400 to win World Series

Reach ALDS / ALCS / World Series : 90.5% / 44.2% / 22.0%

Let the record show that a Rays-Dodgers World Series would be the perfect launching pad into an offseason spent arguing about a salary cap.

For the time being, there is about a 14 percent chance the Rays fail to win the AL East. If that happens, their path to the World Series becomes much more difficult, most likely needing to face Boston in the wild card round before running into the Yankees in the ALDS—with New York holding home-field advantage and a rested pitching staff. We would wish them the best of luck with that.

But if they are able to keep the Yankees at bay and secure the No. 1 seed, their above percentages should increase considerably. At that point, they would have home-field advantage in a best-of-five series against (most likely) whomever survives a Yankees-Red Sox wild card clash.

Getting home-field advantage is big for anyone, but it would be huge for the Rays, sitting at 47-25 in games played at Tropicana Field this season, including a combined 8-2 record against the Yankees and Red Sox.

They would also have home-field advantage—and would figure to be the clear favorite—in the ALCS against whomever emerges from what is shaping up to be, by far, the weakest quadrant of the postseason bracket.

Long story short, it feels like there's about a 40 percent chance they'd win the ALCS if they end up as the No. 1 seed, which they should.

And from there, who knows? They've been much more potent on offense since adding Liam Hicks at the trade deadline and since Chandler Simpson started doing his best Ichiro Suzuki impersonation.

Buy/Sell : Buying the Rays at 22.0% chance of reaching World Series and at +1000 to win World Series

articles.title: MLB Power Rankings as Blue Jays Soar Into Wild Card Mix While Mariners, Orioles Nosedive
articles.summary: The field of viable MLB playoff teams is starting to narrow, and with three full weeks of regular-season baseball remaining, it's make-or-break time for teams on the postseason bubble.
articles.body:
The field of viable MLB playoff teams is starting to narrow, and with three full weeks of regular-season baseball remaining, it's make-or-break time for teams on the postseason bubble.

The Baltimore Orioles and Seattle Mariners were both dealt a major blow last week, while the Toronto Blue Jays are on the come-up and back in the wild-card race.

More shuffling on the fringe awaits in the coming weeks, but teams not currently on the right side of the cut line are running out of time to make their move.

For now, an updated look at the MLB landscape awaits with our weekly power rankings.

In case you missed it, B/R's MLB Power Rankings from last week and all of the power rankings throughout the season can be found at the new MLB Power Rankings hub .

30. Los Angeles Angels (54-89) 29. Colorado Rockies (55-88) 28. San Francisco Giants (59-85) 27. Athletics (57-87) 26. Kansas City Royals (64-80) 25. Detroit Tigers (65-78) 24. Washington Nationals (67-78) 23. New York Mets (65-78)

After a 2-5 week on the road against the Twins and Guardians, the Tigers ' slide to the bottom group is complete. They had a brief surge immediately after their trade deadline sell-off, but have since dropped seven straight series with a 5-17 record during that stretch.

The Athletics taking three of four from the Mariners over the weekend could prove to be the final crushing blow to Seattle's playoff hopes. Despite their ugly overall record, the A's have a 23-20 mark against the rest of the AL West.

Giants slugger Rafael Devers went 10-for-28 with six home runs and 13 RBI in seven games last week, and he is quietly putting together an excellent first full season in San Francisco. The 29-year-old has an .855 OPS with 35 home runs and 91 RBI, leaving him four long balls short of a new career high.

22. Cincinnati Reds (69-74) 21. Minnesota Twins (68-75) 20. Seattle Mariners (67-77) 19. Baltimore Orioles (69-75)

The Orioles and Mariners both went from squarely on the playoff bubble to fighting for their postseason lives in the span of a week. The O's went 1-6 against the Rockies and Red Sox, while the M's dropped three straight to the Athletics before avoiding a sweep on Sunday.

The playoffs may be out of reach, but the Twins at least appear to have found a long-term building block in shortstop Kaelen Culpepper. The 23-year-old is hitting .300/.354/.456 with five doubles, three home runs and 10 RBI in 25 games since making his MLB debut on Aug. 7.

The Reds are still trapped in the NL Central cellar, but series wins over the Padres and Brewers last week were enough for them to climb out of the bottom tier leaguewide. Elly De La Cruz went 10-for-22 last week with two home runs as he puts the finishing touches on a terrific all-around season.

18. Miami Marlins (72-72) 17. St. Louis Cardinals (72-72) 16. Pittsburgh Pirates (71-73)

The Marlins dropped below the .500 mark for the first time since Aug. 7 with their loss to the Cubs on Saturday, and while they rebounded with a win on Sunday, they are running out of time to make a legitimate playoff push. The second-toughest remaining schedule does not help their outlook.

With four consecutive series victories, the Pirates have clawed their way back to the fringe of relevance. Can they survive a road trip to Chicago to face a pair of contending clubs? If they do, their reward is a three-game home series against the Brewers.

Since the Cardinals recalled him from the minors on Aug. 29, Thomas Saggese is 13-for-24 with three doubles, three home runs and eight RBI in eight games while filling in for the injured Masyn Winn at shortstop.

MLB star helps bird off field during game
